invariants: Use the ROOT operation-specific role matrix. Write does not automatically gain Triage operations; Maintain/Admin and organization Owner receive their explicitly stated capabilities.
Private reads require Owner, a valid direct grant, or direct membership in a granted team. Ordinary organization membership and team ancestry grant no private access.
A direct grant replacement stores one record. Revocation removes associated membership/team/grant access without deleting the account.
Registration marks email verified and returns to sign-in. Keep attempted non-sensitive values on rejection and do not echo credentials.
Unknown, wrong-password and unavailable-account sign-in use the same Invalid credentials response and create no session.
Recovery is the fixed local demonstration code 123456, displayed to both known and unknown emails; change credentials only for the associated registered account with valid input.
Sign-out confirmation invalidates only the current browser session. Cancel retains the current page/session. Refresh/back/direct protected entry must re-evaluate active authentication.
File content, branch head, commit history and diff share immutable snapshots. Commit path/content/message/author/parent/target branch as one operation.
Read-only browse/search/compare operations create no branch or commit. A branch selector updates the same current-page branch and file snapshot.
Default-branch change points to an existing branch and retains the previous branch. Protected branches reject direct writes.
Separate title and description save commands. Rejected empty/overlong input leaves the original persisted property unchanged.
Metadata pickers save immediately and close on selection; assignee/label toggle removes only the relationship, and None removes only the milestone association.
Assignable accounts and labels/milestones are validated in the current repository. Historical activity does not count as current metadata.
Close/reopen changes only issue status and activity, preserving title/body/comments/metadata.
Compute comparisons from current base/compare commit snapshots; same/no-difference comparison cannot create a PR, and duplicate Open/Draft pairs cannot create another.
Draft cannot be reviewed or merged. Ready for review changes the same PR to Open without changing identity, branches, commits or title.

Current compare commit invalidates prior review decisions/checks when it changes. Only latest current-commit non-author reviewer decisions affect eligibility; any valid Request changes blocks merging.

At confirmation re-read both heads, conflicts, protection toggles, reviews and current check. Commit merge parents, base head, PR Merged status and merger metadata atomically. Rejection leaves both branch and PR unchanged.
Unprotected branches still reject conflicts and current Request changes; configured approval/test conditions are independently enforced on protected targets.
Close/reopen never updates branch heads. Merged is terminal. Reviewer request removal never removes existing reviews or comments.
The registration page is the form opened by the unique link named “Create an account” from the sign-in page.

The form contains exactly one textbox labeled “Username”, one textbox labeled “Email”, one password input labeled “Password”, one password input labeled “Confirm password”, one initially unchecked checkbox named “Agree to the terms”, and one enabled button named “Create account”.
The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page.
This product directly marks the email of a successfully registered account as verified and does not provide a subsequent email-verification page.
The visitor enters a unique username, email, password, and matching confirmation, checks “Agree to the terms”, and activates “Create account”.

The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters.

The system stores a sign-in-capable account together with its verified-email status and enters the sign-in page; if the username or email conflicts, any field is missing, the email format is invalid, the terms are not accepted, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the system retains the username and email input, displays an itemized message beside the corresponding field, and does not create an account.

The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable.
Visitors can use this capability on the account-access page.
The system validates input rules, displays field errors, and prevents duplicate accounts; on success, it directly creates an available account.

Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read.
For example, a username beginning with a hyphen, email “not-an-email”, password “short”, confirmation “different”, and unchecked terms produce these field errors and preserve the attempted username.
A duplicate username paired with a different unused email displays “Username already exists” and retains both attempted values.

A successful registration accepts a unique username such as “pw-user-<unique suffix>”, its “@example.test” email, and password “Valid-password-123!”; the sign-in form is immediately available, accepts that email, and the resulting signed-in username remains visible after reload.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-1 (Register a New GitHub Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”.
A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages.
The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form.

The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session.

After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.

The password-recovery page is opened by the link “Forgot password” on the sign-in page; the fixed code is displayed as a distinct visible text value exactly “123456”, not only embedded inside a longer instruction.
“Email”, “Verification code”, “New password”, and “Confirm password” are associated field labels;
“Send reset link” and “Reset password” are buttons.

The recovery scenario uses a newly registered account, an unknown email, a compliant replacement such as “Replacement-password-456!”, and invalid code “000000”; failure leaves the registered account able to sign in with its old email/password.
In this flow, the local system does not send email, generate a copyable reset link, or call an external verification-code service.

After the visitor enters an address in the Email field and clicks “Send reset link”, the page directly switches to the next step of the same recovery flow, displays the fixed verification-code text “123456” for local demonstration only, and shows visibly labeled Verification code, New password, Confirm password fields and a “Reset password” button; the page must not require access to email.
To prevent disclosure through the page of whether an account exists, both registered and unknown email addresses enter the same next step and display the same fixed verification code.

The system atomically updates the credentials of that account only when the recovery context is associated with a registered email, the Verification code is character-for-character equal to “123456”, the new password complies with the password rules in REQ-1-1-1, and Confirm password matches it.

If the verification code is wrong, the email is unknown, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the page explains the reason beside the corresponding field and does not modify any account; an incorrect verification code displays “Verification code is invalid”.
After successful submission, the page directly displays “Password updated” and does not produce any email or link.
This local verification code has no email-delivery, expiration, or one-time-link semantics.
Password fields must not echo entered values.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The page contains exactly one button named “Account menu”; its menu contains exactly one link named “Sign out”.
Activating it displays a dialog named “Sign out” with buttons named “Confirm sign out” and “Cancel”.
The dialog explains that sign-out affects only the current browser session.
Only “Confirm sign out” invalidates the session, while “Cancel” or closing the dialog retains the current session and page.

After confirming, refresh, browser back navigation, or directly reopening a previously accessible protected account, repository, or organization page restores an unauthenticated state and displays the “Sign in” link.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

The security form has uniquely labeled password inputs “Current password”, “New password”, and “Confirm password”, and a button “Update password”; submitting an empty current-password field must display the visible application message “Current password is required”.
A failure with an incorrect current password and confirmation “does-not-match” must display the corresponding current-password or confirmation error and leave the old credentials usable.
Each password-change scenario starts with its own verified account in the stated credential state and a different compliant candidate password.

“Password and authentication” is the security page in account Settings used to change the current account credentials; the change affects only the current account's password record and does not alter any other accounts or resources outside the session.
The user must provide the current password, a new password compliant with the REQ-1 password rules, and a character-for-character identical confirmation password; all three fields are required.
The system validates the change, prevents unauthorized updates, and applies the new password to subsequent sign-in attempts.

If the current password is incorrect, the new password is noncompliant, the confirmation does not match, or any field is missing, the system displays the reason in the corresponding field and does not modify the credentials; the applicable visible message is “Current password is incorrect”, “Password confirmation does not match”, or “Current password is required”.
The old password remains valid and the new password must not work for sign-in.

After a successful update, the page displays “Password updated”, the new password is immediately used for subsequent password-based sign-ins, and the old password must no longer work for new sign-ins.
Seed password-change values are `New-password-456!` for the successful update and
`Required-password-789!` for the missing-current-password scenario.
The organization page presents “Repositories” as a navigation link, visually usable as a tab, and a textbox labeled “Find a repository”.
Filtering updates the visible results as the user types, without a separate submit action.
Each result has a link named exactly with the repository name, and opens a heading displaying “organization name/repository name”.
Returning with browser Back keeps the public result available; filtering by the exact private repository name never exposes its link to a visitor.
The seed organization has a public repository and a distinct private repository inaccessible to visitors.

From the organization page, the user clicks the “Repositories” link, can enter a repository name in the filter box, select a public/private filter, and click a repository name in the list to open its overview.
The system displays only the names, descriptions, visibility, and update times of repositories visible to the current user; clicking a result opens that repository's overview.

Visitors can view public repositories on a public organization overview page; signed-in accounts can see only repositories for which they have read permission on the Repositories tab of the organization overview.

The list reads repository name, description, visibility, and update time and provides no write operations; private repositories must first be validated under the already defined repository-access rules.
The account-menu link “Your organizations” opens a page with the link “New organization”.
Its form has fields labeled “Organization name” and “Display name” and a button “Create organization”.
The new overview uses a heading containing the organization identifier, which remains after reload.
Submitting an existing identifier must show “Organization name already exists” even when the display name is also missing; it must not navigate to a heading for the existing organization.
The malformed identifier “-invalid-organization” and a whitespace-only display name are rejected with the applicable field error.
Seed data supplies a verified creator and an existing organization identifier for the duplicate case.
A signed-in user enters a unique organization name and display information on the organization-creation page and confirms.

The organization name must comply with the 1–39-character lowercase ASCII REQ-1 username format and be globally unique; the display name must contain 1–100 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace.

The system validates these rules, creates the organization identifier, display name, and creation time, and saves the current user as both initial owner and member; if the name or display name is noncompliant, the name conflicts, or persistence fails, the system retains non-sensitive input, displays the reason in the corresponding field, and does not create the organization.
The applicable visible message is “Organization name already exists”, “Organization name format is invalid”, or “Display name is required”.

On success, the user is redirected to the new organization overview page, the organization appears in the current user's accessible-organization list, and subsequent team, member, and repository authorization is scoped by that organization identifier.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The organization overview has a “Teams” link; that page has a “New team” link opening the field “Team name” and button “Create team”.
A unique compliant name can be submitted without a description or parent.
The resulting team heading contains its name and remains visible after reload.
Seed data supplies an organization and an account with Owner permission.

A team page is the detail page for a grouping of accounts within an organization, titled “organization name/team name”; the Members tab displays the team's direct members, and Settings is used to change the parent team.
Only an organization Owner can click “New team” from the Teams tab on the organization overview.

The system stores the team identifier, owning organization, name, optional description, optional parent team, creator, and timestamp; if the team name is missing, malformed, duplicated, the parent team does not belong to the current organization, or creation fails, no team is generated.
A malformed team name displays “Team name format is invalid”.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-2-1-2 (Create an Organization After Authentication); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Only an organization Owner may maintain members or hierarchy on an organization team page.
The team maintainer in these scenarios is an organization Owner.
The team page has links “Members” and “Settings”.
On Members, the button “Add member” opens a textbox labeled “Username” and the submit button “Add member”; only the current step's Add member button is exposed as an actionable match.
After adding, the member's complete username is visible once in the member list, alongside a button named “Remove <username>”.
Activating this removal button immediately removes that member without a second confirmation step, and reload keeps the username absent.
Settings contains a native select with combobox role labeled “Parent team”, whose option labels are team names, and a button “Save”.
The original parent remains selected after a rejected change and reload.
The cycle scenario supplies a team with an existing parent and a descendant selectable by name; submitting that descendant shows the cycle error rather than saving it.
The seed record's original-parent value identifies the stored selection, which may differ from its display label.
The membership scenario supplies a current organization member not yet in this team.
On the team page, the Owner clicks “Members” to add or remove current organization members, or selects a new parent team in “Settings” and saves.

The system stores the team-membership relationship or team hierarchy and immediately reflects it in the organization team tree and member list; team hierarchy creates no implicit membership relationship or repository permission, and cyclic hierarchy is prohibited.
A rejected cycle displays “Cyclic team hierarchy is not allowed”.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-2-2-1 (Create an Organization Team); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The organization overview opens “People” through a link.
Its button “Add member” opens the labeled field “Username or email”, a combobox “Role” defaulting to Member, and a submission button “Add member”.
Opening Role exposes clickable options “Member” and “Owner”.
If the opening button remains present, the form submission button follows it in page order.
The successful People list displays the full target username and Member role, with no Pending or Awaiting state; reload preserves the row.
On duplicate or unknown-account failure, keep the form open so the username can be corrected and resubmitted; the existing member's complete username appears only once in the People list.
A separately signed-in new member sees the organization identifier as complete visible text in Your organizations, while an ungranted private repository shows “Access denied”.
The scenarios provide an Owner, a registered nonmember, a different existing member, an unknown username, and a private organization repository with no direct or team grant to the new member.
On the “People” page, an organization Owner clicks “Add member”, enters the username or verified email of an existing account, selects “Member” or “Owner”, and clicks “Add member”.

The system atomically stores the “organization-account-role” membership relationship and immediately displays the organization in both the People list and the target account's “Your organizations” list; the target account can see the organization on its next sign-in, after refreshing the workspace, or after reopening the organization overview.

A Member gains only organization visibility and eligibility to become a candidate for team/repository authorization; an Owner additionally gains Admin permission over the organization and its repositories.

For an existing member, unknown account, unsupported role, or persistence failure, the system displays the reason and does not change the membership relationship; an existing member displays “Account is already a member”, and the unknown username `unknown-reviewer` displays “Account not found”.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-2-1-2 (Create an Organization After Authentication); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Open the organization's “People” link to read member usernames.
Each removable member has a button named “Member menu <username>”; it opens the menuitem “Remove from organization”, followed by the confirmation button “Remove”.
Successful removal makes the complete username absent from People immediately and after reload.
A non-Owner viewing the same member has no member-menu button and no Remove from organization menuitem, rather than merely a disabled control.
Each independent scenario starts with that member present; the non-Owner is an ordinary organization member.
On the “People” page, an organization Owner locates a member, clicks “Remove from organization” in that member's action menu, and clicks “Remove” in the confirmation dialog.

The system atomically deletes that member's organization-membership relationship, all of the account's memberships in teams of that organization, and all direct grants to that account on repositories of the organization; if the account still obtains repository permission through another organization Owner status or an undeleted team grant, effective permission is recalculated according to the valid permission rules, otherwise access is denied.
The system must not delete the personal account, personal repositories, relationships with other organizations, teams themselves, or team grants; the last Owner must not be removed.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-2-1-2 (Create an Organization After Authentication); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
From the repository's “Settings” link, open the “Manage access” link and activate “Add people or teams”.
The picker presents a textbox “Search”, a matching selectable team option whose name contains the team name, a combobox “Role” with clickable role options including “Write”, and an “Add” button.
While the picker is active, hide the opening Add people or teams button from the active view so the submit action is unambiguous.
After saving, the authorization list visibly shows the exact team name and Write role and retains the team after reload.
Existing grants appear as rows whose accessible names include the subject name; each row contains a native select labeled “Role” and a “Save” button.
Selecting the option labeled “Read” and saving replaces Write; after reload exactly one row for the team remains and contains Read.
The creation scenario supplies a repository Admin and an organization team not yet granted access; the replacement scenario supplies a separate repository/team with an existing Write grant.
An organization Owner or repository Admin may grant a repository role of Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, or Admin to a current organization member or team.
In the access-subject picker, matching member or team options update as the administrator types; pressing Enter or activating a separate search button is not required before selecting an option.

A private repository is accessible only to an organization Owner, a member with a direct repository role, or a direct member of a team that has a repository role; an ordinary organization Member has no default private-repository access.
For a given subject and repository, only one direct role grant is stored — saving the same role again does not create a second record, and changing the role replaces the original role.
An account's effective repository role is the highest among Admin from Owner status and all still-valid direct grants and team grants; team hierarchy does not propagate membership or authorization.

The system stores the authorization subject, repository, role, grantor, and timestamp and authorizes operations according to the ROOT role matrix; unauthorized accounts cannot see private repositories.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-2-1-2 (Create an Organization After Authentication) and REQ-2-2-1 (Create an Organization Team); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

The top global search control has searchbox role and accessible name “Search”; entering a repository name and pressing Enter displays repository results directly, without requiring an additional type-filter click.
Each repository result has a link whose accessible name is exactly its repository name, while the result also displays its owner/name metadata.
Clicking it opens a heading containing the repository name; reloading preserves that overview.
A query with no matching repository displays “No results”, including when the visitor returns home and repeats the same query.
Seed data provides a named public repository and a private repository inaccessible to visitors; searching the private name exposes no result link for it.
Visitors or signed-in users can search repositories they are authorized to view.
The system accepts a search query, applies repository-oriented filters or scope constraints, and displays matching repositories with sufficient metadata for the user to open the target repository.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The signed-in workspace provides a “New repository” link.
The form labels are “Owner”, “Repository name”, and “Description”; the signed-in user's personal namespace is selected by default, so it is possible to submit without changing the owner.
Visibility choices are radio controls “Public” and “Private”; initialization is a checkbox “Add a README file”; submission uses the button “Create repository”.
Other defaults must allow duplicate-name and empty-name validation without further input.
A successful initialized private repository shows a heading containing the new name, a visible Private marker, and a README file link; the overview persists after reload.
The optional description “Repository created by Playwright” is saved when entered.
An existing repository in this same default personal namespace is supplied for duplicate validation, which stays on the form and does not open the existing repository heading.

On the repository-creation page, a signed-in user selects a personal or organization owner, enters a repository name and description, selects public or private visibility, and chooses whether to create an initial commit with a README.

The system verifies that the user may create a repository in that owner's namespace, that the name is unique, and that the options are valid; on success, it stores the repository identifier, owner, visibility, default branch, and creator.
If initialization is selected, it must also atomically create the initial branch, README file, and initial commit; failure at any step must leave no partially created repository.
On success, the new repository overview page is opened.
The source overview has a button “Fork”.

The fork form contains a field labeled “Repository name” and button “Create fork”; it defaults to the signed-in user's personal namespace and an allowed visibility, permitting submission after editing only the name.
Seed data supplies a readable source, a user allowed to create personal repositories, and an existing fork name in that namespace for the conflict case.
Success opens a heading containing the new fork name and visible text “Forked from <source repository name>” with a source link; the heading and source relationship survive reload.
On the source repository page, the user clicks “Fork”, selects a target personal or organization namespace, enters an optional new name and visibility, and clicks “Create fork”.
The system creates an independent fork, copies the accessible default-branch history, records the source-repository link, and then opens the new fork overview page.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

A signed-in user can fork only when they have Read or higher permission on the source repository and permission to create repositories in the target personal or organization namespace; when the source repository is private, the fork must remain Private, while a public source repository may be forked as Public or Private.

The system validates permissions on both ends and stores the new fork's owner, visibility, source-repository identifier, default branch, and copied accessible history; if any check fails, no fork is created.
The fork conflict seed uses the existing name `acme-docs-fork` in the target
personal namespace.
The clone popover is opened by a button “Code”, separate from the repository navigation link of the same name.
Protocol controls are tabs “HTTPS” and “SSH”, and the selected clone value has a button “Copy clone value”.
The HTTPS clone value uses the HTTPS protocol; the SSH clone value uses the selected SSH format, including the colon and .git suffix.
Both must identify the current repository.
With browser clipboard permission, copying writes the selected complete value, displays “Copied”, and leaves the repository heading visible.
Seed data provides a visitor-readable public repository; clipboard permission is a browser precondition.
On the repository overview page, the user clicks “Code”, selects the HTTPS or SSH clone method, and then clicks the copy icon to the right of the clone value.
The system writes the selected clone value to the browser clipboard and displays brief “Copied” feedback; this read-only operation does not modify the repository.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Visitors or signed-in users may use this capability on a repository page.
This capability requires the target public object to be available or the user to have view permission.
The system verifies eligibility, displays any required warning or unavailable state, and prevents unauthorized changes.
The selected repository-access value can be pasted by the user into a local tool.
The repository overview identifies the repository in a heading containing “owner/repository name”, displays a visible “Public” marker for a public repository, and provides a navigation link “Code”.
This link is distinct from the clone-menu Code button.
A seeded public repository with its matching name and stable address is readable without sign-in and retains the same heading after reload.
Visitors or authorized users can open a repository overview to confirm repository identity, visibility, description, primary metadata, and available content.
The overview provides the primary entry points for browsing files, viewing repository context, and beginning collaboration.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Open the repository's “Settings” link and then its “General” link to reach Danger Zone.
The visibility action is a button “Change visibility”; the confirmation flow provides a “Public” radio and a button “Confirm visibility”.
Selecting Public and activating Confirm visibility completes the change without requiring the repository name to be retyped or any additional mandatory field.
A non-Admin collaborator must not see the Change visibility button, including when a Settings link is available.
Seed data supplies an Admin, a distinct non-Admin collaborator, and a currently private repository containing public-ready content.
After successful confirmation, a visible Public marker appears, and an unauthenticated visitor reopening the same address sees its repository heading.
A repository administrator changes repository visibility after reviewing the impact on access permissions.
The system blocks unauthorized changes, applies the selected visibility, and enforces the updated access rules when users subsequently open the repository.

Any user with repository-view permission can browse directories and files on the selected branch from the Code page; a directory page displays the current path, while a file page reads the stored content, most recent commit, and file name for that branch and path without creating file changes.
Seed data includes a known directory on the default branch, a known text file immediately inside it, and its expected content.
The directory and file entries are links whose exact accessible names are their respective directory and file names.
Clicking them in order opens the saved text, with the expected content visible as a complete text value; reloading that file page retains the same branch, path, and content.

The repository and file pages each expose one history link named “Commits” (a commit count may accompany the visible label without introducing another matching link).
Seed history includes a known commit message and author, displayed in full as distinct readable text values, and a relative timestamp containing “ago”.
Opening the branch history directly from the repository must show these values without first selecting a file-specific scope.

A seeded commit has an accessible commit entry, a known changed-file path `src/search.ts`, and a readable parent revision.

Opening that commit entry as a visitor displays the changed-file path as an exact text value, the “Changed files” summary, and the numeric additions/deletions summary described below, without requiring previous navigation through history.

The user enters a code keyword in the search box at the top of the repository page and presses Enter, selects the “Code” results page, can further filter by path or language, and clicks a matching file.
The system displays matching snippets, file paths, and branch/revision context within the visible code scope of the current repository; clicking a result opens the corresponding file location.
