The repository page and search results expose one searchbox named “Search”; after Enter, a unique link named “Code” selects code results.
This results-type link must remain distinguishable from repository navigation so the active search page has only one Code link.
Path and language filters are optional, and an unfiltered search can immediately open a result link whose exact accessible name is the matching file name.

Seed data provides the known query `search flow`, a matching file `README.md` with that query visible as a complete text value, and the absent query `no-such-token`, which does not occur in searchable code.
Opening the matching file shows that text; refreshing preserves the file context, text, and a link named exactly after the file.
For the absent query, show “No code results” and retain the exact query in Search.
Returning to the repository and repeating the same search produces the same empty state without stale matches.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

Any user with repository-view permission can use the branch selector at the top of the Code page to list and switch branches; the “current branch” is the branch jointly referenced by the selector, page entry, and file list, not an additionally persisted user setting.
Matching branch options or the “No matching branch” state update as the user types in the branch textbox; pressing Enter or activating a separate search button is not required.
The selector is a unique button named “Branch <current branch name>”; it opens a textbox named “Find branch” and selectable items with role option whose exact accessible names are the branch names.
Seed data includes active branch `main`, target branch `feature-search` containing the file `main-only.md` absent from `main`, and an unknown search term matching no branch.
Selecting the target immediately updates the button's branch name and shows a link with the exact target-only file name.
Escape closes the selector; for an unmatched search it preserves the original active branch before and after reload.
The user opens the branch selector, enters a new branch name, confirms the displayed base branch or commit, and clicks “Create branch: <name>”.
As the user types, a valid unused name displays the “Create branch: <name>” option without requiring Enter or a separate search action, while an invalid name immediately displays “Invalid branch”.
The system creates a new branch pointing to that base commit and switches the selector to it; if the name already exists or the user lacks permission, no branch is created.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-3-1 (List and Switch Repository Branches) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Only signed-in users with Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner status may create branches on repository code and version-control pages;
Read and Triage may only browse.
The system validates the role, stores the new branch name, base commit, creator, and time, and rejects unauthorized requests.
The selector and “Find branch” textbox use REQ-4-3-1's roles.
For a valid unused name, the creation entry has role option and accessible name “Create branch: <name>”.
Its displayed base defaults to the current branch head; selecting this option performs creation and switches branches without a second mandatory confirmation.
Reloading the resulting page entry keeps the newly created branch selected.
In particular, entering `invalid..branch` immediately shows “Invalid branch” and cannot create a reference; generated valid names such as `pw-branch-<unique suffix>` follow the same rules.
A repository administrator enters “Settings” → “Branches”, selects an existing branch from the “Default branch” dropdown, clicks “Update”, and then confirms the change.
The system saves the new default branch and updates the initial branch shown when the repository is newly opened; it does not delete or rewrite the previous default branch.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-3-1 (List and Switch Repository Branches) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Only a repository Admin or organization Owner may change the default branch on repository code and version-control pages; other roles may only view.
The system validates the role, stores the new default branch together with the operator and time, and rejects unauthorized requests.
“Settings” and “Branches” are unique links on their respective pages;
“Default branch” is a native HTML select element exposing the combobox role, with options labeled by exact existing branch names; selecting an option must use the native selection behavior.
The administrator selects a different seeded branch, activates the “Update” button, and then the “Confirm” button in the confirmation dialog.
Opening the repository page entry without a branch then shows “Branch <new default branch name>”; opening that selector still offers an option named exactly after the old default branch.

A non-Admin may have Settings or Branches links hidden or may open a read-only settings page, but no “Default branch” combobox or default-branch update button is rendered for that user; a merely disabled editable selector is insufficient.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The file editor is the form opened from Edit or Add file on the Code page; the user edits file content at a path on the current branch and submits it.
Only Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may submit;
Read and Triage may only view.

A single submission stores the file-path and content change, commit message, author, parent commit, and target branch as one indivisible record and moves the target branch to point to that new commit.

A new or renamed file path must not be empty, must not begin with `/`, must not contain a `..` path segment, and must not conflict with an existing file or directory on the current branch; the commit message must contain 1–72 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace.

If the path conflicts, content validation fails, the commit message is noncompliant, the branch is protected, or persistence fails, the page displays the reason and does not change the file, branch head, or commit history.
An invalid path displays “Invalid file path”, and an empty commit message displays “Commit message is required”.
From the writable Code page, the unique “Add file” button opens the “Create new file” menuitem.
The editor has a field labeled “File name”, a textbox named “File contents”, an initially empty field labeled “Commit message”, and a “Commit changes” button.
Creating a unique file such as `pw-file-<unique suffix>.md` with nonempty text and a message such as `Add <file name>` immediately opens a view displaying the exact saved content.
Its “Commits” link opens history displaying the exact submitted message.
Submitting `../invalid.md` with content `must not be saved` and no commit message reports the invalid path and/or required message and changes neither files nor history.
The example content is ordinary text, not a forbidden content value by itself; rejection follows from the invalid path or missing message.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

Users with repository-view permission can read issue rows for the current repository on the Issues list page; each row references a persisted issue number and displays the title, status, author, labels, and update time.
Users can filter by Open/Closed, title or body keywords, and labels; when the user types in the issue search box, the matching issue rows update without requiring Enter or a separate search button.
Filtering does not create or modify work items.
“Open” and “Closed” are links, not buttons or tabs.
A unique searchbox named “Search issues” filters as the user types, including when the entire seeded title is entered.
Each result title is a link whose exact accessible name is the title.
Open plus the known open title shows that issue and continues to show it after reload;
Closed plus the known closed title shows the closed issue and excludes the open issue.
State and keyword filters combine, and refreshing retains the chosen filter context and matching results.
The seeded closed issue title is `Legacy welcome text`.

An issue detail page is the read view for a uniquely numbered work item within a repository — the top displays the number, a heading whose exact accessible name is the complete title without the issue number, and visible status text “Open” or “Closed”; the body displays the complete saved description as readable text; the right side displays assignees, labels, and milestone; and the bottom displays sections or records containing “Comment” or “Activity” text over time.
Any user with repository-view permission may read this saved data, but the page displays editable controls only to users with the corresponding role.

The seeded open issue title is `Improve onboarding` and its description is `Describe the onboarding improvement.` This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-5-1-1 (List and Filter Repository Issues); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

A signed-in user with Write, Maintain, or Admin clicks “New issue” from the current repository's Issues list page to open the creation form, enters a non-empty title and optional description, and submits.

The system assigns an incrementing unique issue number within the repository, stores the repository identifier, title, description, author, creation time, and Open status, and appends a creation activity; on failure, it does not allocate a number or persist partial data.
On success, the system redirects to the new issue detail page, and the list can locate the issue by its new number and status.
“New issue” is a link on the Issues page.
The creation form has fields labeled “Title” and “Description” and a “Submit new issue” button.
A successful submission displays a heading named exactly after the entered title and the exact saved description; reopening the Issues page entry shows a title link with the same exact name.
A title containing only three spaces is treated as blank; clicking Submit new issue displays “Title is required” and creates no issue, even if the optional description is empty.
Only a signed-in user with Write, Maintain, or Admin may use the unique buttons named “Edit issue title” and “Edit issue description” on an issue detail page.
“Edit issue title” opens a form with a textbox labeled “Issue title” and a button named “Save issue title”;
“Edit issue description” opens a form with a textbox labeled “Issue description” and a button named “Save issue description”.
Read and Triage may only view, these edit controls are unavailable, and the server rejects their submissions.

The system updates only the title or description of the target issue and stores the editor, edit time, and new value, displaying the change in details, list summaries, and the activity timeline; for an empty title, overlong input, or save failure, the original value is retained.
Saving title and description are separate actions; after both saves and reload, the title heading has exactly the new title as its accessible name and the exact new description is visible.

The invalid-edit seed is a separate issue with the original title `Original issue title`; replacing its title with three spaces and activating “Save issue title” shows “Title is required”, and reloading restores the original title heading.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-5-1-2 (View an Issue and Its Discussion); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

Only a signed-in user with Write, Maintain, or Admin may enter a non-empty comment on the issue detail page of the current repository; all signed-in users who can view the issue may add or remove their own reactions on an existing issue or comment.

The system stores the comment identifier, issue identifier, author, body, and creation time, or stores a “subject-target-reaction type” association; for the same user, target, and reaction, only one association is stored, and selecting it a second time removes it.
On success, the new comment or reaction is displayed in the discussion and activity timeline; on failure, no local fake comment or partial reaction is displayed.
The comment editor is labeled “Comment”, and its submit button is named exactly “Comment”.
After submission the complete comment text and author username are visible, and the saved comment remains after reload.
Discussion and activity entries use article semantics so an invalid submission cannot add an article; existing entries remain stable across reload.
For whitespace-only text the Comment button may either be disabled or remain enabled and display “Comment is required” when activated.
Neither path adds a comment or activity.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-5-1-2 (View an Issue and Its Discussion) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

Only a signed-in user with Triage, Maintain, or Admin may click the settings icon in the “Assignees” area on the right side of an issue, search for and check assignable members, or uncheck selected members and close the menu.
Matching assignee options update as the user types in the search textbox; pressing Enter or activating a separate search button is not required before selecting an option.

Assignable members are accounts that have at least Triage permission on the current repository; the system stores the issue-account relationship, operator, and time and records an activity, while non-assignable users do not appear in results.
The settings icon is a button named “Assignees”; the open selector contains a textbox named “Search assignees” and items with role option named exactly after the member username.
Seed data provides an eligible member not initially assigned to the target issue.
Clicking the member option immediately saves the assignment and closes the selector without a separate Save action; the exact username is visible in metadata and remains after reload.

Reopening Assignees shows the selected member without requiring another search; clicking that option again immediately removes the assignment and closes the selector so the username is no longer displayed as an assignee.
Historical assignment and unassignment activities remain historical records.

Unassignment only deletes that issue relationship and does not delete the member account or repository grant; controls are unavailable to users without the role and the server rejects their submissions.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-5-1-2 (View an Issue and Its Discussion); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Only users with Triage, Maintain, or Admin may apply or remove labels that already exist in the current repository; the system stores the issue-label relationship and activity record.
The sidebar has a button named “Labels”, opening options whose exact accessible names are the current repository's label names.
Seed data provides an existing label not yet applied to the target issue.
Clicking its option immediately saves the association and closes the picker, without requiring a separate Save button; the label name is visible on the detail page and remains after reload.
Reopening and selecting the same option removes the association.
The label selector must not create labels, display labels from other repositories, or associate labels from other repositories;
Read and Write users may only view, the control is unavailable, and the server rejects their submissions.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-5-1-2 (View an Issue and Its Discussion); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

On the right side of an issue or pull request, the user clicks the settings icon in the “Milestone” area and selects one item from the current repository's milestone list, or selects “None” to remove the association.
The system stores the association between the work item and milestone and updates detail metadata; it does not create a cross-repository milestone.
The settings icon is a button named “Milestone”, and selectable items have role option with the exact milestone name as their accessible name.
Seed data provides a selectable milestone belonging to the current repository and an issue not yet associated with it.
Clicking the option immediately saves the association and closes the picker with no separate confirmation or save action; the exact milestone name remains visible after reload.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-5-1-2 (View an Issue and Its Discussion); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Only users with Triage, Maintain, or Admin may use this capability on repository planning and issue-management pages;
Read and Write users may only view the current milestone.
The system validates the role and rejects unauthorized submissions.
Only users with Triage, Maintain, or Admin may close or reopen an issue from the issue detail view;
Write and Read users may only view the status.

The system stores the Open or Closed status, operator, and time, records the transition in activity history, and shows it to subsequent viewers; the status transition must not modify the title, description, comments, labels, assignees, or milestone.
The closable seed issue starts Open.
The detail page offers a “Close issue” button when Open and a “Reopen issue” button when Closed; activating either immediately saves the change without an additional confirmation.
Closing displays Closed status and a “Closed issue” activity, and reopening displays Open status.
After reopening and reload the “Close issue” button is available again.
On the separate protected issue, the Read viewer sees neither close nor reopen button; hiding both controls is required, in addition to rejecting unauthorized requests.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-5-1-2 (View an Issue and Its Discussion); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-3-1 (List and Switch Repository Branches) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

A “branch protection rule” is a persistent merge restriction bound to one exact branch name, displayed in the frontend under Settings → Branches, with the backend storing the branch name and rule toggles.
This product supports only two independently selectable requirements: “at least 1 valid Approve from someone other than the PR author” and “required check `test` is success”.
For a given reviewer on the same current compare commit, only the reviewer's latest decision among Comment, Approve, and Request changes counts.
The PR author cannot satisfy the approval requirement; any valid Request changes blocks merging; when the compare branch gains a new commit, all decisions become stale and a new review is required.

“Checks” is the results area on the PR detail page attached to the current compare commit; the `test` status of pending, success, or failure, together with the setter and time, must be stored, and only a repository Admin may update that status from this area.
The system blocks direct writes to a protected branch and applies the rule during subsequent PR merging.
The repository provides a Settings link followed by a Branches link.

The rule form opens from the Add branch protection rule button and contains a field labeled Branch name pattern (an exact branch name, with no wildcard semantics), checkboxes named Require 1 approval and Require status check test, and a Create button; an existing rule uses Save changes.
After saving and reloading, the branch name is visible verbatim with the summaries 1 approval and Require status check test.
For a non-Admin, Add branch protection rule is absent, even if Settings or Branches remain accessible; rejecting a save alone is insufficient.

On the PR detail page, the Checks area is available on arrival, displays test: pending initially, and offers the Admin a combobox named test status with a clickable option named success and a Save button.
Saving displays test: success and identifies the setter and time, and reloading preserves the result for that compare commit.

Seed data comprises a repository Admin and a readable non-Admin account, a dedicated repository and exact branch name with no existing rule before creation, and a separate Open PR targeting protected main with its current test check initially pending.
The Pull requests list page only reads PR records from the current repository; each row displays the number, title, author, status, source branch, and target branch.

Any user with repository-view permission may filter by Draft/Open/Closed/Merged status, author, or review status; filtering only affects the current list display and does not modify PRs, branches, or reviews.
The public list is directly accessible to a visitor and has an Open link for the status filter; selecting it displays the seeded Open PR as a link whose exact accessible name is its title.
Opening that link displays the same title as a heading.
After reloading the filtered list, that Open PR remains visible; leaving the page and reopening the list, then selecting Open again, shows the same PR.
Seed data includes this public list and a stable, uniquely titled Open PR as well as the Closed PR and author used in the filtering scenario.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The PR comparison page is a read-only page shown before creation: base is the target branch that receives the merge result, and compare is the source branch that provides the changes to merge.

A user with Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner status clicks “New pull request” on the “Pull requests” page and selects the two branches; the system calculates comparable commits, changed files, and a diff summary based on the commits they currently point to.
If the branches are the same or there is no difference, the creation entry is disabled; comparison does not save a PR, commit, or branch change.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-3-1 (List and Switch Repository Branches) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Only signed-in users with Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner status may compare branches on the repository pull-request page;
Read and Triage may view existing PRs but cannot enter the creation-comparison flow.
The system validates the role and rejects unauthorized requests.
New pull request is a link.
The comparison page has native select controls with combobox roles named base and compare; each option's visible label is its exact branch name.
Compare changes is a button.
For a valid selection it displays the known changed file path verbatim, a Commit summary with the comparable commit count, and an enabled Create pull request button.
Selecting the same branch in both fields immediately displays No changes and disables the creation button, without requiring Compare changes to be clicked first.
Clicking Compare changes retains that result.
Seed data supplies a contributor with Write permission, a public repository PR-list page entry, a base branch, a distinct compare branch ahead by at least one commit, and a known changed file.
Separate valid comparison page entrys open the same usable creation flow with the branches already selected; these pairs have no existing Open or Draft PR at the start of each creation scenario.
The seeded changed-file path for comparison is `src/search.ts`.
The valid comparison page is directly accessible to the signed-in contributor.

Its Create pull request button opens a form with a field labeled Title, an optional Description field, and a single Create pull request submit button; the comparison-page action is no longer a competing active button.
Successful submission shows the entered title as the exact PR heading and visible Open status, and the title survives reload.
A title containing only spaces is rejected with Title is required and creates no PR.

A user with Write, Maintain, or Admin clicks “Create pull request” on a valid comparison-results page, enters a title containing 1–256 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace and an optional description of at most 65536 characters, confirms distinct base/compare branches with differences, and clicks “Create pull request”.

The system atomically creates an Open PR, stores a unique repository-scoped number, source/target branches, current compare commit, current base commit, title, description, author, creation time, and activity record, and redirects to the detail page; if there is no difference, the branches are the same, a Draft or Open PR with the same source/target pair already exists, the title is empty or overlong, the user lacks permission, or submission fails, no record is created.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-2-2 (Compare Branches Before Opening a Pull Request); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
A visible draft comparison entry offers a Create draft pull request button, which opens the form containing Title and optional Description fields and one Create draft pull request submit button.
Successful creation visibly shows Draft and a present but disabled Merge pull request button.

A dedicated ready-for-review seed PR is separate from draft creation, belongs to the supplied author, initially has no submitted reviews, and displays its title, source branch, and target branch verbatim.
Its Ready for review button changes the same PR to Open; if confirmation is used, it is a single Confirm button.
Afterward the Draft status marker disappears, the title and branches are unchanged, and a Ready for review activity appears;
Open persists on reload.
A user with Write, Maintain, or Admin completes a valid base/compare branch selection, clicks “Create draft pull request”, enters a valid title and optional description, and confirms creation.
The system creates a PR in Draft state using the same persisted fields as a normal PR and displays a “Draft” marker; a draft cannot submit reviews or be merged.

Only the author, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may click “Ready for review” on a Draft detail page to convert it to Open and record an activity; this transition does not change branches, commits, title, or number.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-2-2 (Compare Branches Before Opening a Pull Request); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The PR detail page is the unified read view for the same PR number.
A seeded public Open PR is directly viewable without sign-in and displays its exact title in a heading.
Commits and Files changed are links; the Commits view displays a Commit summary, and the Files changed view displays a Changed files summary.
Reloading preserves the heading and usable navigation links; leaving and reopening the same visible page restores the same PR and allows the same navigation.
Seed data includes its stable title, description, discussion comment, and at least one comparable commit.
Conversation is the timeline for the author's description, ordinary comments, review summaries, and status events;
Commits is the list of commits on the PR's current compare branch relative to base;
Files changed is the entry point to the current diff.
Users with repository-view permission can switch among the three tabs; all read the same persisted PR, branch, and commit data and do not create comments, reviews, or merges.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-2-3 (Create a Pull Request from Comparison Results); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Files changed is the read-only diff view on a PR detail page computed from the current base and compare commits.
From a visible public pull request entry, a visitor activates the Files changed link and sees the known changed file path verbatim and visible aggregate text such as 3 additions, 1 deletions.
This public PR seed contains the same known changed-file path `src/search.ts` supplied for branch comparison, with one added file and one modified file; it requires no sign-in.

Each diff block displays the file path and added/deleted lines; aggregate statistics show the current PR's number of changed files and line counts in the format “<addition count> additions, <deletion count> deletions”.
Users with repository-view permission may expand files or navigate to lines, but this operation does not modify files, commits, branches, comments, or review status.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-3-1 (View Pull Request Overview and Commits); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

An inline review comment is a comment record anchored to a file path, the current compare commit, and a specific added/deleted line in Files changed; it differs from an ordinary comment in Conversation that has no code location.

A user with Write, Maintain, or Admin who is not the PR author can hover over a changed line, click the button visually shown as “+” and accessibly named Add comment, and choose “Add single comment” to publish immediately or “Start a review” to keep it as a pending review draft.
The changed-line Add comment buttons are available for direct activation without a prerequisite hover; the first such button in document order targets the first commentable changed line.
Activating one opens a single editor labeled Comment with Add single comment and Start a review buttons.
Add single comment immediately displays the exact entered body in that diff view and retains it after reload.
Start a review displays the body and Pending review to its author immediately, retains the pending draft after reload, and does not make it public before review submission.
Seed data supplies a non-author Write reviewer, an Open reviewable PR with at least one changed line, and a separate Open PR for the pending-comment scenario.

The system stores the PR, file path, compare commit, line position, author, body, and publication state; when the compare commit changes, published comments are retained but marked Outdated, while drafts are not published automatically.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-3-2 (Inspect Changed Files and Aggregate Diff) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

From the Files changed link, the reviewer activates the Review changes button to open one review form with an optional Summary field, radio controls named Comment, Approve, and Request changes, and a Submit review button.
Selecting Approve and submitting without a summary is valid and displays Approved.
Selecting Request changes with a summary displays Changes requested and that exact summary; the decision remains visible after reload.
Seed data supplies a non-author Write reviewer and separate Open PRs for approval and request-changes submission, with no initial effective decision by that reviewer.
A user who is not the PR author and has Write, Maintain, or Admin may submit Comment, Approve, or Request changes on an Open PR; the author and Draft PRs cannot submit reviews.

The system stores the review decision, reviewer, current compare commit, optional explanation, and time; a new decision by the same reviewer replaces that reviewer's effective decision for the current commit while preserving the old record.
Approve is valid only when the reviewer is not the author and the compare commit is still the same;
Request changes blocks merging until that reviewer submits a new Comment or Approve for the current compare commit, or the compare branch receives a new commit that makes the old decision stale.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-3-1 (View Pull Request Overview and Commits) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The Reviewers button opens a picker with a textbox named Search.
Typing an eligible username immediately reveals an option with that exact accessible name.
Selecting the option saves the request immediately without a separate Save action, closes the picker, and displays the username in the reviewer area; it remains after reload.
Each requested reviewer has a button named Remove followed by a space and the username; clicking it immediately removes the request and the username from that area, without a confirmation step.

The seed PR is Open, belongs to the signed-in author, and initially has no request or submitted review from the eligible target reviewer; the target is a distinct non-author collaborator with Write or higher permission.
Removing a request persists across reload.

A “reviewer request” is a pending-review relationship between a PR and a candidate reviewer account, displayed in the Reviewers area on the right side of the PR detail page; it is not the same as a submitted review decision.
The author of an Open or Draft PR, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may create or delete this relationship.
Matching reviewer options update as the user types in the search textbox; pressing Enter or activating a separate search button is not required before selecting an option.

A candidate reviewer must have Write, Maintain, or Admin on the repository and must not be the PR author; the system stores or deletes the “PR-reviewer request” relationship together with the operator and time.
Removing a request does not delete reviews, comments, or activity records already submitted by that user and does not change the user's effective review decision.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-2-3 (Create a Pull Request from Comparison Results) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
On an eligible PR, Merge pull request and then Confirm merge are buttons; confirming displays Merged, and that state remains after reload.
A blocked PR keeps a visible disabled Merge pull request button and explains its unmet review or protection condition before any click.
Seed data supplies a Maintain account and separate Open PRs for success and refusal.
The eligible PR targets protected main, has a current non-author approval and test: success, and has no conflicts.
The blocked PR targets a protected branch and lacks the required valid approval; its disabled button is accompanied by Review required by branch protection.
Each seed state is restored independently before reuse.
“Merge” is the only write operation that writes the current compare commit's changes from an Open PR into the base branch; it is not simply marking the PR as complete.

Only Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may merge from the PR detail page using the sole supported “Create a merge commit” method; the merge confirmation area should display satisfied and unsatisfied conditions.

Before confirmation, the system rereads the target branch head, current compare commit, merge-conflict state, and protection rules — there must be no valid Request changes; if the target is protected, each enabled rule requirement is enforced independently, requiring 1 valid non-author Approve for the current compare commit when Require 1 approval is enabled and requiring `test` success when Require status check test is enabled.
An unprotected target has no additional approval-count or check-success requirement, but merging still requires no merge conflicts and no valid Request changes review.

After validation succeeds, the system atomically creates a merge commit whose parents are the target-branch head at merge time and the current compare commit, updates the target-branch head, sets the PR to Merged, and stores the merger, time, and resulting commit identifier.

If any condition is unsatisfied or persistence fails, the page explains the applicable reason and neither the target branch nor PR changes; a missing required approval displays “Review required by branch protection”.
Merged is terminal.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-3-4 (Submit a Pull Request Review) and REQ-6-1 (Protect Branches with Review and Status-Check Requirements); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The PR page provides Close pull request and Reopen pull request as buttons for authorized users.
Close pull request immediately sets Closed without an extra confirmation dialog, then Reopen pull request immediately restores Open.
After reload, Close pull request is available again.
For a viewer who is neither author nor Maintain/Admin/Owner, both controls are absent, rather than merely disabled or rejected after activation.
Seed data supplies the author and a separate Read viewer, an authored Open PR for the close/reopen cycle, and a separate Open PR readable by that viewer for permission validation.

When the proposed change should not proceed, the PR author, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may close an unmerged Open or Draft PR without merging; the same roles may reopen a Closed PR as Open.

The system stores the status, operator, and time and records the transition, while keeping the PR discussion, reviews, diff, and branch references viewable; closing or reopening must not update any branch.
Merged is terminal, the page does not display close or reopen operations, and the server rejects status changes.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-2-3 (Create a Pull Request from Comparison Results) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
This product is a simplified GitHub collaboration platform.

Unless an atomic requirement explicitly allows more than one role, every quoted user-interface name is the exact English accessible name of the control; the role, scope, and observable-state rules stated by each atomic requirement are authoritative.
Values described as existing accounts, organizations, teams, repositories, branches, files, commits, issues, milestones, pull requests, reviews, and permission relationships are predefined seed data.

The application must provision those records before the corresponding scenario and supply each account through an isolated browser session; they are not extra features that a participant must expose through a private API.
Generated names may contain a unique suffix, but their role, ownership, visibility, and relationships are exactly those stated in the atomic requirement.
Every atomic requirement remains enabled even when seed configuration is incomplete.
All write operations must be persisted on the server, checked against the current session and target-object permission, and completed atomically.

Organization Owner, repository Admin, Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, and Admin permissions follow the operation-specific rules in the requirements below; these roles are not an automatic cumulative ladder.
Real-time collaboration, Actions, Packages, Wiki, project boards, notification delivery, and external Git remote protocols are outside the scope of this product.
This module defines the “account” and “session” required to access the system.

An account is a persistent individual identity storing a username, verified email, and credential status; a session is a record created after successful account sign-in that represents only the current browser login state.
Visitors enter the account-access page from “Sign up”, “Sign in”, or “Forgot password” on the home page; signed-in users enter security settings or sign out from the account menu.
The account menu is the control in the upper-right corner of the page that displays the current signed-in account, organization list, and sign-out entry.
No page, error message, or recovery flow may display a full password.

After successful sign-in, the account menu displays the current user, and subsequent organization, repository, issue, and pull-request pages use this session to determine visibility and operation permissions; sign-out, password changes, and recovery must immediately change the session state visible to subsequent requests.

The account-access page is the shared page used by unauthenticated users to register, sign in, and recover a password, with the frontend showing the appropriate form and submit button for each operation.

The local product does not implement an email-verification page, email delivery, or an external verification-code service — successful registration directly stores a sign-in-capable account and marks its email as verified; successful sign-in only stores a new session and does not create a duplicate account; after submitting an email for password recovery, the page directly displays the fixed verification code `123456` and the password-reset form, and only the correct code together with a compliant new password updates the password of the same account.

Registration, sign-in, and recovery pages must use visible labels to identify fields and submit actions; after failure, non-sensitive input is retained, while password and password-confirmation fields must not redisplay submitted values.

Signed-in users enter the organization list through “Your organizations” in the account menu and can create or open an organization; visitors can only view public repositories through public organization pages.
The organization overview provides Repositories, People, and Teams entries.
An organization Owner directly adds or removes members on People, creates teams and maintains hierarchy on Teams, and grants roles to members or teams in Manage access under repository Settings.

Organization membership only determines whether a user can see the organization and can be a candidate for team/repository authorization; it does not automatically grant access to any private repository.
Access to a private repository comes only from organization Owner status, a direct role grant on that repository, or direct membership in a team authorized for that repository.
All changes must be reflected simultaneously in organization details, people/team lists, and the actual access results of affected repositories.
The organization overview page uses the organization name as a heading; its “Repositories”, “People”, and “Teams” navigation entries have link roles even when visually styled as tabs.
The Repositories tab lists repositories owned by the organization, the People tab lists members and their Member/Owner roles, and the Teams tab lists teams.
This module supports visitors discovering an organization's public repositories and signed-in accounts creating organizations from the “Your organizations” page.

The unique organization name uses the same globally unique 1–39-character lowercase ASCII format as the REQ-1 username; the display name must contain 1–100 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace.

After successful creation, the system stores the organization object and the creating account's Owner membership relationship, and the user enters the new organization overview page; subsequent team, member, and organization-repository authorization is scoped by this organization identifier.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
On the current organization's member- and team-management pages, users create teams, maintain team hierarchy and membership relationships, and directly add or remove organization members.

A team name contains 1–50 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens, may not begin or end with a hyphen, and must be unique within the same organization; a team must belong to an organization, and a parent team must belong to the same organization and may not create a direct or indirect cycle.

Organization membership and team membership are independent persisted relationships; team hierarchy is used only for display and management and does not implicitly add members of a parent or child team to the other team.

On the People page, an Owner enters the username or verified email of an existing account and confirms, after which the system immediately saves that account's Member or Owner membership relationship; there is no invitation, Pending, or acceptance step.

When removing a member, the system atomically deletes that organization-membership relationship, all of that account's team memberships in the organization, and all direct grants to that account on repositories of the organization; team grants themselves are not deleted.

If removal would leave the organization with no Owner, the system rejects the operation and keeps all relationships unchanged; the person's account, personal repositories, and relationships with other organizations must not be deleted.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-2-1-2 (Create an Organization After Authentication); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
A repository is a container for code, branches, commits, files, and collaborative work items.

The repository overview page is titled “owner/repository name”, displays the owner, name, Public/Private marker, description, and default branch, and provides Code, Issues, Pull requests, and Settings entries; the “owner” is an individual account or organization, and a repository belonging to an organization is an organization repository.

Users open a repository overview from global search results, a personal/organization Repositories list, or a direct link; signed-in users with creation permission create a personal or organization repository from “New repository”.

Public repositories allow visitor Read access; private personal repositories allow access only to their owner and explicitly authorized subjects; private organization repositories allow access only to organization Owners, members with direct repository roles, or direct members of teams with repository roles, and ordinary organization Members do not automatically gain access merely through membership.
After visibility or access grants change, search, lists, direct links, and repository pages must all use the same access rule.
The repository-creation page is the form opened by “New repository”, where the user selects an owner, name, visibility, and initialization options.

A “fork” is an independent repository copied from a readable source repository — the frontend displays the source link on the fork overview page, and the system stores the source-repository identifier; branches and commits in the fork may evolve independently and never write back to the source repository.
A “clone page entry” is a read-only address displayed in the repository Code popover and can be copied to the clipboard; it does not mean this product implements an external Git protocol.
Both new repositories and forks must enter a browsable repository overview page.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

The Code page is the main page for browsing code in a repository — the top of the page displays the current branch selector, the main area displays files and directories at the current path on the current branch, clicking a file opens a read-only file page, and clicking Commits opens commit history.
A file is content at a path on a branch; a directory is only a path hierarchy used for organization and is not an independent collaboration object.
A branch is a named reference pointing to a commit, and switching branches only changes the file snapshot read by the current page.

A commit is an immutable change record that stores the parent commit, author, message, time, and changed files; users with Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner permission can create new commits from a file page through Edit or Add file.
Every file, commit, comparison, and branch page displays the repository and current branch or revision.
Editing a file must create a new commit and must not rewrite historical content.

Seed data for read-only scenarios consists of public repositories and directly openable repository, file, and commit pages; visitors need not sign in to browse files, history, diffs, code search, or existing branches.

Write scenarios provide separate existing contributor accounts with Write or higher permission on their target repositories and an unprotected writable branch; default-branch scenarios provide an Admin and a separate readable non-Admin account.

These accounts sign in through the home-page “Sign in” link, the “Username or email” and “Password” fields, and the “Sign in” button; the signed-in username is visible before opening the target repository entry.
Unless a narrower scope is explicitly given below, each named control is unique on the active page, and field and option names refer to accessible names.

The “commit history” page displays commit records for a branch or file path in reverse chronological order; the “diff” page compares the file contents of two commits or revisions line by line, where base is the earlier or target revision and compare is the newer or to-be-compared revision; the “code search” page searches for keywords only within readable file content in the current repository.
All three are read-only views that do not create commits or modify files or branches and follow repository visibility and access permissions.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
The branch selector is the control at the top of the Code page that lists and switches branches; the system stores a unique name and current pointed-to commit for each branch.
Creating a branch creates a new named reference at a specified base commit; it does not copy files or rewrite base history.
The default branch is the branch read by default when opening the repository overview or a repository entry without a specified branch; it is not the only existing or writable branch.

A branch name is 1–255 characters and may contain only ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.`, and `/`; it must not end with `/` or `.`, and must not contain consecutive `..` or `//`; duplicate names, invalid names, or lack of permission must prevent branch creation.
Changing the default branch must not alter existing branches, commits, or source/target references of already-open PRs.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
An issue is a persistent work item within a repository used to record pending work, a defect, or a discussion topic; it is not a code file or PR.

The Issues page is the list page in repository navigation; each row displays the issue number, title, Open/Closed status, author, and labels, and clicking the number or title opens the issue detail page.

At the top of the detail page are the title and status; the right side displays Assignees, Labels, and Milestone metadata in order; the main area displays the description, comments, and activity timeline.
The “activity timeline” is an append-only history that records creation, edits, comments, assignment, labels, milestone, and status changes in chronological order.

A label is a pre-existing colored classification name in the current repository; a milestone is a pre-existing goal-classification item in the current repository that may be associated with multiple issues or PRs but does not change their content or status.
Write, Maintain, and Admin may create issues, edit titles/descriptions, and comment;
Triage, Maintain, and Admin may assign participants, apply labels, set milestones, and close or reopen issues;
Read may only view.

Every operation is performed around a unique issue number within the repository, and the detail page and list display the same persisted data; after refresh, re-login, or opening from another account with view permission, the same record is still read.
For issue operations, the explicit role lists in this module define eligibility per operation rather than an implicit cumulative grant from a role's name;
Write can create, edit, and comment but cannot assign, label, set milestones, or change status.
Organization Owners act with Admin permission.

Read-only seed scenarios provide a public repository's visible Issues entry, distinct Open and Closed issues with known titles, and an issue entry with known title, description, metadata, and discussion.

Mutation scenarios provide isolated issues for successful editing, invalid-title editing with a known original title, commenting, comment validation, assignment, labels, milestone, and closing; their initial states must not be changed by another scenario.
The author and commenter accounts have Write or higher permission; the editor used for both content and metadata operations has Maintain or Admin permission.
A separate viewer has Read permission on a protected issue.
All authenticated scenarios use the home-page “Sign in” link, fields labeled “Username or email” and “Password”, and the “Sign in” button, after which the signed-in username is visible.
Named controls below are unique on the active page unless a narrower scope is stated; detail pages and reloads must work independently of earlier list navigation.
The Issues list page displays issues within the current repository; status, keyword, and label filters only change the rows currently displayed in the browser and do not write or delete issues.

The issue detail page is the complete view of the work item with the same number, aggregating the description, right-side metadata, comments, and activity timeline, and also serves as the common entry point for editing, commenting, assigning, labeling, setting milestones, and closing/reopening.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
Supports creating issues in the current repository, editing titles and descriptions, and appending discussion comments.

An issue title contains 1–256 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace; the description may be empty and is at most 65536 characters; a comment contains 1–65536 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace.

After successful creation, the issue is assigned a unique repository-scoped number and the detail page opens; editing changes only the current fields of the target issue, while comments are appended to the activity timeline as independent records with author and timestamp.
On insufficient permission, empty required fields, overlong input, or persistence failure, the system must not create an empty issue, overwrite the original description, or append a partial comment.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-5-1-2 (View an Issue and Its Discussion); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

An “Assignee” is an account assigned to follow up on an issue and is displayed on the right side of the detail page; it only stores an association between the issue and account and does not change that account's repository permission.
A “Label” is a preconfigured classification name in the current repository and is displayed in the frontend as a label badge; it only stores an association between the issue and label.

A “Milestone” is a preconfigured stage or version goal in the current repository and is displayed as single-select metadata on the right side; a work item may be associated with at most one milestone, and selecting None deletes that association.
This version provides no page or interface for creating, editing, or deleting labels or milestones; seeded data and initial repositories must provide selectable items.
Each relationship addition or removal updates the details and activity record and does not automatically create cross-repository labels, milestones, or membership relationships.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-5-1-2 (View an Issue and Its Discussion); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
A pull request (PR) is a persistent proposal to “merge code changes from the compare branch into the base branch”; it is not a branch, commit, or issue.
The Pull requests page lists the current repository's PR number, title, author, source/target branches, and status;

“New pull request” first opens the comparison page, where the user selects base (the target branch that receives the changes) and compare (the source branch that provides the changes) and inspects the diff.
On the PR detail page, Conversation displays the title, description, ordinary comments, activities, and review summary;
Commits displays commits on the compare branch relative to base;
Files changed displays per-file, per-line differences;
Checks displays check status for the PR's current compare commit.

A PR's persisted status may only be Draft, Open, Closed, or Merged — normal creation produces Open, draft creation produces Draft, and the author or Maintain/Admin may mark a Draft as Ready for review to transition it to Open; the author or Maintain/Admin may transition an unmerged Open or Draft PR to Closed and may transition Closed back to Open;
Merged is terminal and cannot be closed or reopened.
Write, Maintain, and Admin may add inline comments and submit reviews, the author or Maintain/Admin may request reviewers, and only Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may merge.
Each PR stores a repository-scoped number, source/target branches, creation-time and current compare commits, creation-time base commit, title, description, author, status, and activity records.

When the compare branch receives a new commit, the system updates the current compare commit, marks all existing review decisions as stale while preserving them in the timeline, recalculates merge eligibility, and retains inline comments at their original commit and line position marked Outdated.
Failure does not change branches or PR state.
The following REQ-6 interaction contracts use English accessible names and apply to direct navigation as well as navigation from a repository.
Each named action, field, and navigation link is unique on its active page unless explicitly repeated per changed line or reviewer.
PR titles are headings whose accessible name is exactly the persisted title; list titles are links with that same exact name.
Conversation, Commits, Files changed, and Checks are navigation links, even when visually styled as tabs.
The current PR status is visible text.

Signed-in scenarios begin with the unique Sign in link on the home page, labeled Username or email and Password fields, a Sign in button, and the account username visible after authentication; each role account has a username, verified email, and password.
Visitor scenarios use public repositories and require no session.

Seed records identify the corresponding pages, not to private implementation interfaces; role accounts, branches, PRs, and mutable state must be provisioned and restored independently for each scenario, including repeated and parallel runs.
Existing titles, usernames, paths, and branch names described below are supplied as seed values and must be displayed verbatim; generated PR titles and comments may carry a unique suffix.

Supports listing and filtering pull requests in the current repository, selecting source/target branches to view comparison results, and creating a normal or draft pull request from a valid comparison.
Read may only view;
Write, Maintain, and Admin may create PRs.

Comparison results are temporary read-only context on the creation page; after successful creation, the system persists the source/target branches, current compare commit, creation-time base commit, title, description, author, and status, then opens the new pull-request detail page.

Creation must be rejected without leaving a partial record when source and target are the same, there are no comparable commits, the same repository already has a Draft or Open PR with the same source/target pair, or the user lacks creation permission.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-3 (Branch Management); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

Supports viewing the overview, commits, changed files, and diffs on a pull-request detail page, and adding review comments or submitting review decisions on specific files and line ranges in the diff.
Read may view; users with Write, Maintain, or Admin who are not the PR author may comment on an Open PR and submit Comment, Approve, or Request changes;
Draft does not allow review submission.
An inline comment must store the target PR, compare commit, file path, line position, author, and body; a review decision must store the reviewer, current compare commit, status, and explanation.
Each reviewer has only one effective decision on a given current compare commit; a new decision replaces the reviewer's effective decision while preserving history.
Viewing operations are read-only, and if comment or review submission fails, it must not be displayed as published.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-2-3 (Create a Pull Request from Comparison Results); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

commands.name: Register a New GitHub Account
preconditions: The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page.

The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters.

The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable.

Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read.

A successful registration accepts a unique username such as “pw-user-<unique suffix>”, its “@example.test” email, and password “Valid-password-123!”; the sign-in form is immediately available, accepts that email, and the resulting signed-in username remains visible after reload.
effects: The registration page is the form opened by the unique link named “Create an account” from the sign-in page.

The form contains exactly one textbox labeled “Username”, one textbox labeled “Email”, one password input labeled “Password”, one password input labeled “Confirm password”, one initially unchecked checkbox named “Agree to the terms”, and one enabled button named “Create account”.
The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page.
This product directly marks the email of a successfully registered account as verified and does not provide a subsequent email-verification page.
The visitor enters a unique username, email, password, and matching confirmation, checks “Agree to the terms”, and activates “Create account”.

The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters.

The system stores a sign-in-capable account together with its verified-email status and enters the sign-in page; if the username or email conflicts, any field is missing, the email format is invalid, the terms are not accepted, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the system retains the username and email input, displays an itemized message beside the corresponding field, and does not create an account.

The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable.
Visitors can use this capability on the account-access page.
The system validates input rules, displays field errors, and prevents duplicate accounts; on success, it directly creates an available account.

Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read.
For example, a username beginning with a hyphen, email “not-an-email”, password “short”, confirmation “different”, and unchecked terms produce these field errors and preserve the attempted username.
A duplicate username paired with a different unused email displays “Username already exists” and retains both attempted values.

A successful registration accepts a unique username such as “pw-user-<unique suffix>”, its “@example.test” email, and password “Valid-password-123!”; the sign-in form is immediately available, accepts that email, and the resulting signed-in username remains visible after reload.
